vignette:
Kiet Nguyen is a 40-year-old journalist who, until two years ago, had built his career covering human rights abuses across Southeast Asia. The assignment that changed everything was a deep-dive into a military-linked trafficking network in a border region. He had been careful, had cultivated sources for months, but someone had talked. He was taken from a guesthouse at night, blindfolded, and held for six days. His captors wanted to know who else he had spoken with, what evidence he had already filed. They had methods. He remembers the sound of a generator starting up just before the interrogations began, and the way the room would spin when he was forced to stand for hours after being beaten. He remembers the names they used when they spoke about him in the third person—"the writer," "the spy," "the one who thinks he can tell our story." What he cannot remember, no matter how hard he tries, are the faces of the men who held him down during the worst of it. There are gaps in the memory, whole stretches of time that feel like a film reel with missing frames. When he tries to deliberately recall the sequence of events, his mind goes blank, and what he does retrieve feels so extreme that he sometimes wonders if it actually happened to him at all. The story feels unreal, like something he read about someone else.

In the months after he was released and repatriated, Kiet tried to return to his life. He went back to his desk at the newspaper, but he could not sit still. He found himself watching his colleagues too closely, scanning their faces for signs of threat, certain that any of them could be an informant. He stopped answering calls from old contacts in the region, and then stopped seeing the friends he had socialised with before the event altogether. He told himself they would not understand, that they would look at him and see what had been done to him. He had come to believe that others could read his history on his face—that his trauma was written visibly on his skin, that anyone who looked at him long enough would know he had been broken. This belief followed him into every room. He became certain there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person, that he had been defective all along and the torture had simply revealed it. Most crushing of all was what he had done to survive. He had given them names. He had told them everything they wanted to know. He had acted in ways that went against every principle he had ever held about loyalty and integrity, and he could not forgive himself for it. He dwelled on this constantly, running the event over in his mind, imagining how he could have held out longer, how he could have been stronger, how he could have prevented the whole thing from unfolding the way it did.

His body began to betray him in small ways first. He would be sitting at his desk, and a child would cry in the hallway outside his apartment, and his heart would slam against his ribs before his conscious mind had even registered the sound. Ordinary noises—a door slamming, a chair scraping against a floor—made him jump so violently that he once knocked a coffee cup off his own desk. The dizziness came without warning, usually when he was standing still in a line or waiting for an elevator, and he would feel the room tilt and his vision blur, and he would have to brace himself against a wall. He started to associate this physical sensation with the feeling of being about to be grabbed, and so he began to avoid any situation where he might have to stand still. He stopped taking the subway. He stopped going to grocery stores. He stopped leaving his apartment at all unless it was absolutely necessary.

His eating became erratic. He found that if he did not eat, he felt lighter, more in control, less likely to be caught off guard. Hunger became a kind of anchor—a predictable sensation in a world that felt unpredictable. Over six months, he lost nearly thirty pounds. His editor at the newspaper called to check on him. Kiet let the call go to voicemail. He did not call back. The divorce had already happened before the assignment, but now the isolation was total. What finally brought him to seek help was a Tuesday morning in October. He was standing in his kitchen, dizzy, having not eaten in two days, and a child in the building next door began to cry. He heard the name of one of his captors—or a name that sounded close to it—shouted in the street below. He realised he had not spoken a single word aloud in four days. He was afraid of what he might do if he stayed alone any longer. He was also afraid of what it would mean to tell a stranger the full story—afraid that saying it out loud would make it real, that the therapist would see it on his face, that he would be judged as harshly as he judged himself. But he made the call anyway, because the alternative felt worse.
